## The Question

When a square matrix has an inverse, multiplying in either order gives the identity matrix. For a rectangular matrix, both products can still be formed. They just have different sizes.

Let $A$ be an $m\times n$ real matrix. A *left inverse* is an $n\times m$ matrix $L$ with $LA=I_n$. A *right inverse* is an $n\times m$ matrix $R$ with $AR=I_m$. Here $I_d$ is the $d\times d$ identity matrix.

If $m\ne n$, could both equations hold, even if we choose different matrices for $L$ and $R$?

## A Proof Using Rank

The rank of a matrix is the dimension of its column space, the span of its columns. It is also the dimension of its row space, the span of its rows. Both dimensions equal the number of pivots after row reduction.

Let $B$ be an $n\times k$ matrix, so $AB$ is $m\times k$. The diagrams use $m=3$, $n=2$, and $k=4$. The height of $AB$ matches $A$, and its width matches $B$.

### Read a Column of the Product

Pick a column $b_j$ of $B$. Column $j$ of $AB$ is $Ab_j$. If $a_1,\ldots,a_n$ are the columns of $A$, then
$$
Ab_j=\sum_{\ell=1}^{n} b_{\ell j}a_\ell.
$$
The entries you read down $b_j$ are the weights for the columns of $A$.

Every column of $AB$ therefore belongs to the column space of $A$. Taking the span gives $\operatorname{col}(AB)\subseteq\operatorname{col}(A)$, so $\operatorname{rank}(AB)\leq\operatorname{rank}(A)$.

### Read a Row of the Product

Now pick row $i$ of $A$. Let $r_\ell$ be row $\ell$ of $B$. Row $i$ of $AB$ is
$$
\sum_{\ell=1}^{n} a_{i\ell}r_\ell.
$$
This time, read across the row of $A$ to get the weights for the rows of $B$.

Every row of $AB$ belongs to the row space of $B$. Thus $\operatorname{row}(AB)\subseteq\operatorname{row}(B)$, so $\operatorname{rank}(AB)\leq\operatorname{rank}(B)$. Together the two bounds give
$$
\operatorname{rank}(AB)\leq\min\{\operatorname{rank} A,\operatorname{rank} B\}.
$$

### Apply the Two Bounds

A matrix with $m$ rows and $n$ columns has at most $\min\{m,n\}$ pivots. If $LA=I_n$, then
$$
n=\operatorname{rank}(LA)\leq\operatorname{rank}(A)\leq n.
$$
So a left inverse requires $\operatorname{rank}(A)=n$. If $AR=I_m$, then
$$
m=\operatorname{rank}(AR)\leq\operatorname{rank}(A)\leq m.
$$
So a right inverse requires $\operatorname{rank}(A)=m$. Both equations can hold only if $m=n$.

## A Proof Using Linear Maps

A matrix with $n$ columns and $m$ rows defines a linear map $T_A:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^m$ by $T_A(x)=Ax$. Writing $x$ in coordinates gives
$$
Ax=x_1a_1+\cdots+x_na_n.
$$
Each output is a linear combination of the columns of $A$. Conversely, any such combination is an output. Just use its coefficients as the entries of $x$. This is why the image of $T_A$, the set of all its outputs, is exactly $\operatorname{col}(A)$.

### What Each Inverse Does

If $LA=I_n$, then $T_L\circ T_A=\mathrm{id}_{\mathbb R^n}$. Applying $A$ and then $L$ returns the original input. If $Ax=Ax'$, applying $L$ gives $x=x'$. So $T_A$ is *injective*: different inputs give different outputs.

If $AR=I_m$, then $T_A\circ T_R=\mathrm{id}_{\mathbb R^m}$. Given any $y\in\mathbb R^m$, choose $x=Ry$. Then $Ax=y$. So $T_A$ is *surjective*: every vector in its target space is an output.

### Compare the Dimensions

If $T_A$ is injective, its kernel (the set of inputs sent to zero) contains only the zero vector. The rank–nullity theorem then gives $\dim\operatorname{im}(T_A)=n$. If $T_A$ is surjective, its image is all of $\mathbb R^m$, so that same dimension is $m$. Hence $m=n$ if both inverses exist.

## Two Left Inverses for One Matrix

Consider the map $A(x,y)=(x,y,0)$ from $\mathbb R^2$ to $\mathbb R^3$. The maps
$$
\begin{aligned}
L_1(x,y,z)&=(x,y),\\
L_2(x,y,z)&=(x+z,y)
\end{aligned}
$$
are distinct, but both return $(x,y)$ when applied to $A(x,y)=(x,y,0)$. They are both left inverses.

There is no right inverse. The third coordinate of every output of $A$ is zero, so a target such as $(0,0,1)$ can never be reached. A rectangular matrix can have several inverses on one side, even though it cannot have an inverse on each side.
